plays.play_title: The atheist's tragedie: or The honest man's reuenge As in diuers places it hath often beene acted. Written by Cyril Tourneur.

speeches.speaker: D'amuille.
verse: I Saw my Nephew Charlemont, but now
Part from his Father. Tell him I desire
To speak with him.
Borachio, thou art read
In Nature and her large Philosophie.
Obseru'st thou not the very selfe same course
Of reuolution both in Man and Beast?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The same. For birth, growth, state, decay and death:
Onely, a Man's beholding to his Nature
For th'better composition o'the two.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: But where that fauour of his Nature, is
Not full and free; you fee a man becomes
A foole, as little-knowing as a beast.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: That showes there's nothing in a Man, aboue
His nature; if there were, consid'ring t'is
His beings excellencie, t'would not yeeld
To Natures weakenesse.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Then if Death casts vp
Our totall summe of ioy and happinesse;
Let me haue all my sences feasted in
Th'abundant fulnesse of delight at once,
And with a sweet insensible increase
Of pleasing surfet melt into my dust.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: That reuolution is too short me thinkes.
If this life comprehends our happinesse,
How foolish to desire to dye so soone?
And if our time runnes home vnto the length
Of Nature, how improuident it were
To spend our substance on a minutes pleasure,
And after liue an age in miserie?

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: So thou conclud'st that pleasure onely flowes
Vpon the streame of riches.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Wealth is Lord
Of all felicitie.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: T'is Oracle.
For what's a man that's honest without wealth?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Both miserable and contemptible.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Hee's worse Borachio. For if Charitie
Be an essentiall part of Honestie,
And should be practis'd first vpon our selues;
Which must be graunted; then your honest man
That's poore, is most dishonest, for hee is
Vncharitable to the Man, whom hee
Should most respect. But what doth this touch me,
That seeme to haue enough? Thankes industrie.
T'is true. Had not my Body spredde it selfe
Into posteritie; perhaps I should
Desire no more increase of substance, then
Would hold proportion with mine owne dimentions.
Yet euen in that sufficiencie of state,
A man has reason to prouide and adde.
For what is he hath such a present eye,
And so prepar'd a strength; that can fore-see,
And fortifie his substance and himselfe,
Against those accidents, the least whereof
May robbe him of an ages husbandry?
And for my children; they are as neere to me,
As branches to the tree whereon they grow;
And may as numerously be multiplied.
As they increase, so should my prouidence;
For from my substance they receiue the sap,
Whereby they liue and flowrish.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Sir enough,
I vnderstand the marke whereat you aime.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Silence. Ware interrupted. Charlemont!

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Good morrow Vncle.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Noble Charlemont;
Good morrow. Is not this the honour'd day
You purpos'd to set forward to the warre?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: My inclination did intend it so.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: And not your resolution?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Yes my Lord;
Had not my Father contradicted it.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: O noble warre! Thou first originall
Of all man's honour. How deiectedly,
The baser Spirit of our present time
Hath cast it selfe below the ancient worth
Of our forefathers! From whose noble deedes
Ignobly we deriue our pedigrees.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Sir, taxe not me for his vnwillingnesse.
By the command of his authoritie,
My disposition's forc'd against it selfe.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Nephew, you are the honour of our bloud.
The troope of Gentry, whose inferiour worth
Should second your example, are become
Your Leaders: and the scorne of their discourse,
Turnes smiling backe vpon your backewardnesse.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: You neede not vrge my spirit by disgrace
T'is free enough. My Father hinders it.
To curbe me, hee denyes me maintenance
To put me in the habite of my ranque.
Vnbinde me from that strong necessitie,
And call me Coward if I stay behind.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: For want of meanes? Borachio! Where's the gold?
I'de disinherite my posteritie
To purchase honour. T'is an interest
I prize aboue the principall of wealth.
I'm glad I had th'occasion to make knowne
How readily my substance shall vnlocke
It selfe to serue you. Here's a thousand Crownes.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: My worthy vncle; in exchange for this,
I leaue my bond. So I am doubly bound;
By that for the repayment of this gold,
And by this gold to satisfie your loue.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Sir; t'is a witnesse (onely) of my loue;
And loue doth alwayes satisfie it selfe.
Now to your Father; labour his consent.
My importunitie shall second yours.
Wee will obtaine it.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: If intreatie faile,
The force of reputation shall preuaile.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Goe call my Sonnes, that they may take their leaues
Of noble Charlemont. Now my Borachio!

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The substance of our former argument
Was wealth.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: The question how to compasse it.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Young Charlemont is going to the warre.

speeches.speaker: Dam.
verse: O, thou begin'st to take me.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Marke me then.
Me thinkes, the pregnant wit of Man, might make
The happy absence of this Charlemont,
A subiect for commodious prouidence.
He has a wealthy Father; ready eu'n
To drop into his graue. And no mans power
When Charlemont is gone, can interpose
'Twixt you and him.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Th'ast apprehended; both
My meaning and my loue. Now let thy trust,
For vndertaking and for secrecie,
Hold measure with thy amplitude of wit;
And thy reward shall paralell thy worth.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: My resolution has already bound
Mee to your seruice.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: And my heart to thee.
Here are my Sonnes.—
There's my eternitie. My life in them;
And their succession shall for euer liue.
And in my reason dwels the prouidence,
To adde to life as much of happinesse.
Let all men lose, so I increase my gaine,
I haue no feeling of anothers paine.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I prithee let this current of my teares,
Diuert thy inclination from the warre.
For of my children thou are onely left,
To promise a succession to my house.
And all the honour thou canst get by armes,
Will giue but vaine addition to thy name;
Since from thy auncestours thou dost deriue
A dignitie sufficient; and as great
As thou hast substance to maintaine and beare.
I prithee stay at home.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: My noble Father.
The weakest sigh you breath, hath power to turne
My strongest purpose; and your softest teare
To melt my resolution to as soft
Obedience. But my affection to the warre,
Is as heriditary as my bloud,
To eu'ry life of all my ancestry.
Your predecessours were your presidents;
And you are my example. Shall I serue
For nothing but a vaine Parenthesis,
I'th'honour'd story of your Familie?
Or hang but like an emptie Scutcheon,
Betweene the trophee's of my predecessours.
And the rich Armes of my posteritie?
There's not a French-man of good bloud and youth'
But eyther out of spirit or example,
Is turn'd a Souldier. Onely Charlemont
Must be reputed that same heartlesse thing,
That Cowards will be bold to play vpon.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Good morrow my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Morrow good brother.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Good morrow Vncle.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Morrow knide Nephew.
What? ha'you wash'd your eyes wi'teares this morning?
Come: by my soule his purpose does deserue
Your free consent. Your tendernesse disswades him.
What to the Father of a Gentleman,
Should be more tender then the maintenance
And the increase of honour to his house?
My Lord; here are my Boyes. I should be proud
That eyther this were able, or that inclin'd
To be my Nephewes braue competitor.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your importunities haue ouercome.
Pray God my forc'd graunt proue not ominous.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: We haue obtain'd it.—Ominous? in what?
It cannot be in anything but death.
And I am of a confident beliefe,
That eu'n the time, place, manner of our deathes,
Doe follow Fate with that necessitie;
That makes vs sure to dye. And in a thing
Ordain'd so certainly vnalterable,
What can the vse of prouidence preuaile?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Morrow my Lord Montferrers, Lord D'amville.
Good morrow Gentlemen. Couzen Charlemont!
Kindly good morrow. Troth I was afeard
I should ha come too late, to tell you that
I wish your vndertakings a successe
That may deserue the measure of their worth.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: My Lord; my dutie would not let me goe,
Without receiuing your commandements.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Accomplements are more for ornament,
Then vse. Wee should imploy no time in them,
But what our serious businesse will admit.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your fauour had by his duty beene preuented,
If we had not with-held him in the way.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Hee was o'comming to present his seruice.
But now no more. The Cooke inuites to breakfast.
Wilt please your Lordship enter.—Noble Lady.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: My noble Mistresse! this accomplement
Is like an elegant and mouing speech,
Compos'd of many sweete perswasiue points,
Which second one onother, with a fluent
Increase, and confirmation of their force,
Reseruing still the best vntill the last,
To crowne the strong impulsion of the rest
With a full conquest of the hearers sense:
Because th'impression of the last we speake
Doth alwayes longest and most constantly
Possesse the entertainment of remembrance.
So all that now salute my taking leaue,
Haue added numerously to the loue,
Wherewith I did receiue their courtesie.
But you (deare Mistresse) being the last and best
That speakes my farewell; like th'imperious cloze
Of a most sweete Oration, wholy haue
Possess'd my liking, and shall euer liue
Within the soule of my true memory.
So (Mistresse) with this kisse I take my leaue.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: My worthy Seruant! you mistake th'intent
Of kissing. T'was not meant to separate
A paire of Louers; but to be the seale
Of Loue; importing by the ioyning of
Our mutuall and incorporated breathes,
That we should breath but one contracted life.
Or stay at home, or let me goe with you.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: My Castabella! for my selfe to stay,
Or you to goe, would either taxe my youth
With a dishonourable weakenesse, or
Your louing purpose with immodestie.
And for the satisfaction of your loue,
Heere comes a man whose knowledge I haue made
A witnesse to the contract of our vowes,
Which my returne by marriage shall confirme.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
I salute you both with the spirit of copulation, ^
already informed of your matrimoniall purposes, and will ^
testimonie to the integritie.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O the sad trouble of my fearefull soule!
My faithfull seruant! did you neuer heare,
That when a certaine great man went to th'warre,
The louely face of heau'n was masqu'd with sorrow,
The sighing windes did moue the breast of earth,
The heauie cloudes hung downe their mourning heads,
And wept sad showers the day that hee went hence,
As if that day presag'd some ill successe,
That fatallie should kill his happinesse;
And so it came to passe. Me thinkes my eyes
(Sweet Heau'n forbid) are like those weeping cloudes,
And as their showers presag'd so doe my teares,
Some sad euent will follow my sad feares.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Fie, superstitious? is it bad to kisse?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: May all my feares hurt me no more then this.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
Fie, fie, fie, these carnall kisses doe stirre vp the
Concupisences of the flesh.

speeches.speaker: Leuid.
verse: O! heer's your daughter vnder her seruants lips.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Madame, there is no cause you should mistrust
The kisse I gaue, t'was but a parting one.

speeches.speaker: Leuid.
verse: A lustie bloud! Now by the lip of Loue
Were I to choose, your ioyning one for mee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Your Father stayes to bring you on the way.
Farewell. The great commander of the warre
Prosper the course you vndertake. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: My Lord! I humbl^ take my leaue—Madame!
I kisse your hand.—And your sweet lip.—Farewell.
Her power to speake is perish'd in her teares.
Something within me would perswade my stay,
But Reputation will not yeeld vnto 't.
Deare Sir, you are the man whose honest trust
My confidence hath chosen for my friend.
I feare my absence will discomfort her.
You haue the power and opportunitie
To moderate her passion. Let her griefe
Receiue that friendship from you; and your Loue
Shall not repent it selfe of courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
Sir, I want words and protestation to insinuate into
your credit; but in plainnesse and truth, I wil quallifie her griefe
with the spirit of consolation.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Sir, I will take your friendship vp at vse.
And feare not that your profit shall be small;
Your interest shall exceede your principall.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Mounsieur Languebeau! Happily encountred. The
honestie of your conuersation, makes me request more int'rest
in your familiaritie.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
If your Lordship will be pleased to salute me without
ceremonie, I shall be willing to exchange my seruice for your
fauour; but this worshipping kinde of entertainment, is a superstitious
vanitie; in plainnesse and truth I loue it not.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
I embrace your disposition; and desire to giue you
as liberall assurance of my loue, as my Lord Belforest your deserued
fauourer.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
His Lordship is pleased with my plainnesse and truth
of conuersation.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
It cannot displease him. In the behauiour of his noble
daughter Castabella; a man may read her worth and your instruction.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
That Gentlewoman is most sweetly modest, faire, honest,
handsome, wise, well-borne, and rich.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: You haue giuen me her picture in small.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
Shee's like your Dyamond; a temptation in euery
mans eye, yet not yeelding to any light impression her selfe.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: The praise is hers; but the comparison your owne.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: You shall forgiue me that, Sir.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
I will not doeso much at your request as forgiue you
it. I will onely giue you it Sir. By—You will make mee
sweare.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
O! by no meanes. Prophanemot your lippes with the
foulnesse of that sinne. I will rather take it. To saue your oath,
you shall lose your Ring.—Verily my Lord; my praise came
short of her worth. Shee exceedes a Iewell. This is but onely
for ornament; Shee both for ornament and vse.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Yet vnprofitably kept without vse. Shee deserues a
worthy Husband, Sir. I haue often wish'd a match betweene
my elder Sonne and her. The marriage would ioyne the houses
of Belforest and Damville into a noble alliance.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: And the vnitie of Families is a worke of loue and charitie.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
And that worke an imployment well becomming
the goodnesse of your disposition.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
If your Lordship please to impose it vpon mee; I will
carry it without any second end, the surest way to satisfie your
wish.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Most ioyfully accepted.—Rousard! Here are
Letters to my Lord Belforest touching my desire to that purpose.

speeches.speaker: Rousard!
prose:
I send you a suitor to Castabella. To this Gentlemans
discretion I commit the managing of your suite His good successe
shall be most thankefull to your trust. Follow his instructions,
he will be your leader.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: In plainnesse and truth.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
My leader? does your Lordship thinke mee too weake
to giue the on-set my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I will onely assist your proceedings.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
To say true, so I thinke you had neede, for a sicke
man can hardly get a womans good will without help.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: This giues mee feeling of a better suite.
prose:
Charlemont! thy gratuitie and my promises were both
but words; and both like words shall vanish into ayre.—For
thy poore empty hand I must be mute:

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Borachio! didst precisely note this man?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: His owne profession would report him pure.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: And seemes to know if any benefit,
Arises of religion after death;
Yet but compare's profession with his life;
They so directly contradict themselues,
As if the end of his instructions were
But to diuert the world from sinne, that hee
More easily might ingrosse it to himselfe.
By that I am confirm'd an Atheist.
Well! Charlemont is gone. And here thou seest,
His absence the foundation of my plot.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Hee is the man whom Castabella loues.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: That was the reason I propounded him
Employment fix'd vpon a forraine place,
To draw his inclination out o'th'way.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: T'has left the passage of our practise free.

speeches.speaker: D'am
verse: This Castabella is a wealthy heire,
And by her marriage with my elder Sonne;
My house is honour'd, and my state increas'd.
This worke alone deserues my industry:
But if it prosper, thou shalt see my braine
Make this but an induction to a point
So full of profitable policie;
That it would make the soule of honestie
Ambitious to turne villaine.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I bespeake
Employment in't. I'le be an instrument
To grace performance with dexteritie.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Thou shalt. No man shall rob thee of the honour.
Goe presently and buy a crimson Scarfe,
Like Charlemonts. Prepare thee a disguise,
I'th'habite of a Souldiour, hurt and lame;
And then be ready at the wedding feast,
Where thou shalt haue imployment in a worke
Will please thy disposition.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: As I vow'd;
Your instrument shall make your proiect proud.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: This marriage will bring wealth. If that succeede,
I will increase it though my Brother bleed.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
Nay good Sir; in troth if you knew how little it pleases
mee, you would forbeare it.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
I will not leaue thee, till th'ast entertain'd mee for thy
seruant.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
My seruant? You are sicke you say. You would taxe
mee of indiscretion to entertaine one that is not able to doe me
seruice.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
The seruice of a Gentlewoman consists most in chamber
worke, and sicke men are fittest for the chamber. I pr^thee
giue me a fauour.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
Mee thinkes you haue a very sweet fauour of you
owne.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: I lacke but your blacke eye.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
If you goe to buffets among the Boyes, they'l giue
you one.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
Nay if you grow bitter, Ile dispraise your blacke eye.
The gray eie'd Morning makes the fairest day.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
Now that you dissemble not, I could be willing to
giue you a fauour. What fauour would you haue?

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: Any toy: any light thing.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
Fie. Will you be so vnciuill to aske a light thing at a
Gentlewomans hand?

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: Wilt giue mee a bracelet o'thy haire then?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: Doe you want haire Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
No faith Ile want no haire, so long as I can haue it for
mony.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: What would you doe with my haire then?

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: Weare it for thy sake sweet hart.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: Doe you thinke I loue to haue my haire worne off?

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: Come you are so witty now, and so sensible.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: Tush. I would I wanted one o'my sences now.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: Bitter againe? What's that? Smelling?

speeches.speaker: Casta
prose:
No, no, no. Why now y'are satisfied I hope. I haue
giuen you a fauour.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: What fauour? a kisse? I prithee giue mee another.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: Shew mee that I gaue you then.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: How should I shew it?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
You are vnworthie of a fauour if you will not bestow
the keeping of it one minute.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
Well in plaine termes, doest loue mee? That's the
purpose of my comming.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: Loue you? Yes Very well.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: Giue mee thy hand vpon't.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
Nay, you mistake mee. If I loue you very well, I
must not loue you now. For now your are not very well, y'are
sicke.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: This Equiuocation is for the iest now.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
I speak't as t'is now in fashion, in earnest. But I
shall not be in quiet for you I perceiue, till I haue giuen you
a fauour. Doe you loue mee?

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: With all my hart.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose:
Then with all my hart, Ile giue you a Iewell to hang
in your eare,—Harke yee—I can neuer loue you.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
Call you this a Iewell to hang in mine eare? T'is no
light fauour, for Ile be sworne it comes somewhat heauily to
mee. Well. I will not leaue her for all this. Mee thinkes it
animates a man to stand too't, when a woman desires to be rid
of him at the first sight.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I entertaine the offer of this match;
With purpose to confirme it presently.
I haue already moou'd it to my daughter;
Her soft excuses sauour'd at the first
(Me thought) but of a modest innocence
Of bloud; whose vnmoou'd streame was neuer drawne
Into the current of affection. But when I
Replyed with more familiar arguments,
Thinking to make her apprehension bold;
Her modest blush fell to a pale dislike,
And shee refus'd it with such confidence,
As if shee had beene prompted by a loue
Inclining firmely to some other man,
And in that obstinacie shee remaines.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
Verily that disobedience doth not become a Childe.
It proceedeth from an vnsanctified libertie. You will be accessarie to your owne dishonour if you suffer it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Your honest wisedome has aduis'd mee well.
Once more Ile moue her by perswasiue meanes.
If shee resist; all mildenesse set apart,
I will make vse of my authoritie.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
And instantly, least fearing your constraint; her contrary
affection teach her some deuise that may preuent you.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: To cut off eu'ry opportunitie,
Procrastination may assist her with;
This instant night shee shall be marryed.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Best.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Please it your Lordship, my mother attends
I'th' Gallerie, and desires your conference.
This meanes I vs'd to bring mee to your eare.
Time cuts off circumstance; I must be briefe.
To your integritie did Charlemont
Commit the contract of his loue and mine.
Which now so strong a hand seekes to diuide:
That if your graue aduise assist me not,
I shall be forc'd to violate my faith.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
Since Charlemont's absence, I haue waighed his loue
with the spirit of consideration; and in sinceritie I finde it to be
friuolous and vaine. With-draw your respect; his affection deserueth
it not.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Good sir; I know your heart cannot prophane
The holinesse you make profession of;
With such a vitious purpose, as to breake
The vow, your owne consent did help to make.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
Can he deserue your loue, who in neglect of your delightfull
conuersation; and in obstinate contempt of all your
prayers and teares; absents himselfe so far from your sweet fellowship,
and with a purpose so contracted to that absence, that
you see hee purchases your separation with the hazard of his
bloud and life; fearing to want pretence to part your companies?—T'is rather hate that doth diuision moue; Loue still desires
the presence of his Loue.—Verily, hee is not of the
Familie of Loue.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O doe not wrong him. T'is a generous minde
That ledde his disposition to the warre:
For gentle loue and noble courage are
So neare allyed; that one begets another:
Or, Loue is Sister, and Courage is the Brother.
Could I affect him better then before,
His Souldiers heart would make me loue him more.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: But Castabella.—

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Tush, you mistake the way into a woman,
The passage lyes not through her reason, but her bloud.
Nay, stay! How wouldst thou call the childe,
That being rais'd with cost and tendernesse,
To full habilitie of body and meanes;
Denies reliefe vnto the parents, who
Bestow'd that bringing vp?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Vnnaturall.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Then Castabella is vnnaturall.
Nature the louing mother of vs all,
Brought forth a woman for her owne reliefe;
By generation to reuiue her age.
Which now thou hast habilitie and meanes
Presented; most vnkindly dost deny.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Belieue me Mother; I doe loue a man.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Preferr'st th' affection of an absent Loue,
Before the sweet possession of a man;
The barren minde before the fruitfull body;
Where our creation has no reference
To man; but in his body: being made
Onely for generation; which (vnlesse
Our children can be gotten by conceit)
Must from the body come. If Reason were
Our counsellour, wee would neglect the worke
Of generation, for the prodigall
Expence it drawes vs too of that which is
The wealth of life. Wise Nature (therefore) hath
Reseru'd for an inducement to our sence,
Our greatest pleasure in that greatest worke.
Which being offer'd thee; thy ignorance
Refuses, for th'imaginarie ioy
Of an vnsatisfied affection, to
An absent man. Whose bloud once spent i'th'warre;
Then hee'l come home, sicke, lame and impotent;
And wed thee to a torment; like the paine
Of Tantalus, continuing thy desire,
With fruitlesse presentation of the thing
It loues; still moou'd, and still vnsatisfied.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Now Leuidulcia! Hast thou yet prepar'd
My Daughters loue to entertaine this Man?
Her husband here?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I'm but her mother i'law;
Yet if shee were my very flesh and bloud,
I could aduise no better for good.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose:
Sweet wife! Thy ioyfull husband thus salutes
Thy cheeke.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: My husband? O! I am betraid.—
Deare friend of Charlemont! your puritie
Professes a diuine contempt o'th'world;
O be not brib'd by that you so neglect,
In being the worlds hated instrument,
To bring a iust neglect vpon your selfe!—
Deare Father! let me but examine my
Affection.—Sir, your prudent iudgement can
Perswade your sonne that t'is improuident
To marry one whose disposition, he
Did ne'er obserue.—Good sir, I may be of
A nature so vnpleasing to your minde;
Perhaps you'l curse the fatall houre wherein
You rashly marryed me.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: My Lord Belforest!
I would not haue her forc'd against her choise.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Passion o'me thou peeuish girle. I charge
Thee by my blessing, and th'authoritie
I haue to claime th'obedience; marry him.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Now Charlemont! O my presaging teares!
This sad euent hath follow'd my sad feares.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: A rape, a rape, a rape!

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: How now?

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Why what is't but a Rape to force a wench to marry,
since it forces her to lie with him she would not?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Verily, his Tongue is an vnsanctified member.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Verily, your grauitie becomes your perish'd soule, as
hoary mouldinesse does rotten fruit.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Couzen, y'are both vnciuill and prophane.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Thou disobedient villaine; get thee out of my sight.
Now by my Soule Ile plague thee for this rudenesse.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Come; set forward to the Church.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
And verifie the Prouerbe. The nearer the Church;
the further from God.—Poore wench. For thy sake, may
his habilitie die in his appetite; that thou beest not troubled

with him thou louest not. May his appetite moue thy desire to
another man: so hee shall helpe to make himselfe Cuckold.
And let that man be one that he payes wages too: so thou shalt
profit by him thou hatest. Let the Chambers be matted, the
hinges oyl'd, the curtaine rings silenced, and the chamber-maid
hold her peace at his owne request, that he may sleepe the quietlier.
And in that sleepe let him be soundly cuckolded. And
when hee knowes it, and seekes to sue a diuorce; let him haue
no other satisfaction then this: Hee lay by and slept: the Law
will take no hold of her, because he wink'd at it.

speeches.speaker: Leuidulcia.
prose: MIstresse Cataplasma! I expected you an houre since.

speeches.speaker: Cata.
prose:
Certaine Ladies at my house (Madame) detain'd
mee; otherwise I had attended your Ladiship sooner.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Wee are beholding to you for you companie. My
Lord; I pray you bid these Gentlewomen welcome: th'are my
inuited friends.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Gentlewomen, y'are welcome, pray sit downe.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Frisco! by my Lord D'amville's leaue I prith^ goe
into the Buttry. Thou sha't finde some o'my men there; if they
bid thee not welcome, they are very Loggerheads.

speeches.speaker: ^res.
prose:
If your Logger heads will not, your Hoggesheads shall
Madame, if I get into the Buttry.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
That fellowes disposition to mirth should be our present
example. Let's be graue and meditate, when our affaires require
our seriousnes. T'is out of season to be heauily disposed.

speeches.speaker: Len.
prose: We should be all wound vp into the key of Mirth.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: The Musicke there.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose:
Where's my Lord Montferrers? Tell him here's a
roome attends him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose:
Heauen giue your marriage that I am depriu'd of,
ioy.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
My Lord Belforest! Castabella's health.

Set ope' the Sellar dores, and let this health goe freely round
the house.—Another to your Sonne, my Lord; To noble
Charl. mont. Hee is a Souldier. Let the Instruments of warie
congratulate his memorie.—

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose:
My Lord, here's one i'th'habite of a Souldier saies hee
is newly return'd from Ostend, and has some businesse of import
to speake.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Ostend! let him come in. My soule fore-tels hee
brings the newes will make our Musicke full. My brothers ioy
would doe't: and here comes hee will raise it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose:
O my spirit, it does disswade my tongue to question
him, as if it knew his answere would displease.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Souldier! what newes? wee heard a rumour of a blow
you gaue the enemie.

speeches.speaker: Bor
prose: T'is very true my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Canst thou relate it.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: I Prithee doe.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The enemie, defeated of a faire
Aduantage by a flattring stratagem;
Plants all th' Artillerie against the Towne.
Whose thunder and lightning made our bulwarkes shake;
And threatned in that terrible report,
The storme wherewith they meant to second it.
Th'assault was generall. But for the place
That promis'd most aduantage to beforc'd;
The pride of all their Army was drawne forth,
And equally diuided into Front,
And Rere. They march'd. And comming to a stand,
Ready to passe our Channell at an ebbe,
W^aduis'd it for our safest course, to draw
Our ^uices vp and mak't vnpassable.
Our Gouernour oppos'd; and suffered'em
To charge vs home e'en to the Ramp^ers foot.
But when their front was forcing vp our breach,
At push o'pike, then did his pollicie
Let goe the sluices, and trip'd vp the heeles
Of the whole bodie of their troupe, that stood
Within the violent current of the streame.
Their front beleaguer'd twixt the water and
The Towne; seeing the floud was growne too deepe,
To promise them a safe retreate; expos'd
The force of all their spirits, (like the last
Expiring gaspe of a strong harted man)
Vpon the hazard of one charge; but were
Oppress'd and fell. The rest that could not swimme,
Were onely drown'd; but those that thought to scape
By swimming, were by murtherers that flankerd,
The leuell of the floud both drow'nd and slaine.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Now by my soule (Souldier) a braue seruice.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: O what became of my deare Charlemont?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Walking next day vpon the fatall shore,
Among the slaughter'd bodies of their men,
Which the full-stomack'd Sea had cast vpon
The sands, it was m'vnhappy chance to light
Vpon a face, whose fauour when it liu'd
My astonish'd minde inform'd me I had seene.
Hee lay in's Armour; as if that had beene
His Coffine, and the weeping Sea (like one;
Whose milder temper doth lament the death
Of him whom in his rage he slew) runnes vp
The Shoare; embraces him; kisses his cheeke,
Goes backe againe and forces vp the Sandes
To burie him; and eu'rie time it parts,
Sheds teares vpon him; till at last (as if
It could no longer endure to see the man
Whom it had slaine, yet loath to leaue him;) with
A kinde of vnresolu'd vnwilling pace,
Winding her waues one in another, like
A man that foldes his armes, or wrings his hands
For griefe; ebb'd from the body and descends:
As if it would sinke downe into the earth,
And hide it selfe for shame of such a deede.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: And Souldier; who was this?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: O Charlemont!

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Your feare hath told you that whereof my griefe
Was loath to be the messenger.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
prose: O God.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Charlemont drown'd? Why how could that be? since
it was the aduerse partie that receiued the ouerthrow.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: His forward spirit press'd into the front;
And being engag'd within the enemie,
When they retreated through the rising streame;
I'the violent confusion of the throng
Was ouerborne and perish'd in the floud.
And here's the sad remembrance of his life,—The Scarfe.
Which for his sake I will for euer weare.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Torment me not with witnesses of that,
Which I desire, not to beleeue; yet must.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Thou art a Scrichowle; and dost come i'night
To be the cursed messenger of death.
Away. Depart my house; or (by my soule)
You'l finde me a more fatall enemie,
Then euer was Ostend. Be gone. Dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Sir t'was my loue.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Your loue to vexe my heart with that I hate?
Harke, doe you heare? you, knaue?—
O th'art a most delicate sweete eloquent villaine^

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Was't not well counterfaited?

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Rarely.—Be gone. I will not here reply.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Why then farewell. I will not trouble you.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: So. The foundation's laid. Now by degrees,
The worke will rise and soone be perfected.
O this vncertaine state of mortall man!

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: What then? it is th'ineuitable fate
Of all things vnderneath the Moone.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: T'is true.
Brother for healths sake ouercome your griefe.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I cannot sir. I am vncapable
Of comfort. My turne will be next. I feele
My selfe not well.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: You yeeld too much to griefe.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
All men are mortall. The houre of death is vncertaine.
Age makes sicknesse the more dangerous. And griefe is
subiect to distraction. You know not how soone you may be
depriu'd of the benefit of sense. In my vnderstanding (therefore)
you shall doe well if you be sicke to set your state in present
order. Make your Will.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: I haue my wish.—Lights for my Borther.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Ile withdraw a while;
And craue the honest counsell of this man.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: With all my heart. I pray attend him sir.
This next roome please your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Where you will.

speeches.speaker: Leuid.
prose:
My Daughter's gone. Come Sonne. Mistresse Cataplasma,
come; wee'l vp into her chamber. I'de faine see how she
entertaines the expectation of her husbands bedfellowship.

speeches.speaker: Rou.
prose:
'Faith howsoeuer shee entertaines it; I shall hardly
please her; therefore let her rest.

speeches.speaker: Le^id.
verse: Nay, please her hardly and you please her best.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: Boy! fill some drinke Boy.

speeches.speaker: Fresco.
prose: Enough good Sir; not a drop more by this light.

Not by this light? Why then put out the candles and
wee'l drinke i'the darke and t'wut old Boy.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: No^ no, no, no, no.
Why then take thy liquour. A health Fresco.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: Your health will make me sicke sir.
Then t'will bring you o'your knees I hope sir.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: May I not stand and pledge it sir?
I hope you will doe as wee doe.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: Nay then indeed I must not stand, for you cannot.
Well said old boy.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
Old boy, you'l make me a young childe anon: for if
I continue this, I shall scarce be able to goe alone.
My body is as weake as water, Fresco.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
Good reason sir, the beere has sent all the malt vp into
your braine, and left nothing but the water in your body.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Borachio! seest those fellowes?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Yes my Lord.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Their drunkennesse that seemes ridiculous,
Shall be a serious instrument, to bring
Our sober purposes to their successe.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: I am prepar'd for th'execution, sir.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Cast off this habite, and about it straight.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose:
Let them drinke healthes, & drowne their braines i'the floud;
Ile promise them they shall be pledg'd in bloud.
You ha'left a damnable snuffe here.
Doe you take that in snuffe Sir?
You are a damnable rogue then.—

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Fortune I honour thee. My plot still rises,
According to the modell of mine owne desires.—
Lights for my Brother.—What ha'you drunke your selues
mad you knaues.
My Lord the Iackes abus'd mee.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
I thinke they are the Iackes indeed that haue abus'd
thee, Dost heare? that fellow is a proud knaue. Hee has abus'd
thee. As thou goest ouer the fields by and by, in lighting my
brother home, Ile tell thee what'sha't doe. Knocke him ouer
the pate with thy torch, Ile beare the out in't.
I will sindge the goose by this torch.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Doest heare; fellow. Seest thou that proud knaue, I
haue giuen him a lesson for his sawcinesse. H'as wrong'd thee.
Ile tell thee what'sha't doe: As we goe ouer the fields by and
by, clap him sodainely o'er the coxe-combe with thy torch,
Ile beare thee out in't.
I will make him vnderstand as much.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Now Mounsieur Snuffe! What has my brother done?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
D'am.
prose:
Yes. Let him if he can.—Ile make it sure from
his reuoking.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Brother now good night.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: The skie is darke, wee'l bring you o'er the fields.
Who can but strike, wants wisedome to maintaine:
Hee that strikes safe and sure, has heart and braine.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O Loue! thou chast affection of the Soule,
Without th'adultrate mixture of the bloud;
That vertue which to goodnesse addeth good:
The min^on of heauens heart. Heauen! is't my fate
For louing that thou lou'st to get thy hate?
Or was my Charlemont thy chosen Loue?
And therefore hast receiu'd him to thy selfe?
Then I confesse thy anger's not vniust.
I was thy riuall Yet to be diuorc'd
From loue, has beene a punishment enough.
(Sweete heauen) without being marryed vnto hate,
Hadst thou beene pleas'd: O double miserie!
Yet since thy pleasure hath inflicted it,
I^ not my heart, my dutie shall submit.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Mistresse Cataplasma, good night. I pray when your
Man has brought you home, let him returne and light me to
my house.

speeches.speaker: Cata.
prose: He shall instantly waite on your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Good Mistresse Cataplasma; for my seruants are all
drunke; I cannot be beholding to'em for their attendance.

O here's your Bride.

speeches.speaker: Rous.
prose: And melancholique too, me thinkes.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: How can shee choose? your sicknesse will
Distaste th'expected sweetnesse o'the night.
That makes her heauie.

speeches.speaker: Rou.
verse: That should make her light.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Looke you to that.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: What sweetnesse speake you of?
The sweetnesse of the night consists in rest.

speeches.speaker: Rou.
verse: With that sweetnesse thou shalt be surely blest,
Vnlesse my groning wake thee. Doe not moane.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Sh'ad rather you would wake, and make her grone.

speeches.speaker: Rou.
verse: Nay'troth sweete heart, I will not trouble thee.
Thou shalt not lose thy maiden-head too night.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O might that weakenesse euer be in force;
I neuer would desire to sue diuorce!

speeches.speaker: Rou.
verse: Wilt goe to bed.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: I will attend you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rou.
verse: Mother, good night.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Pleasure be your bed-fellow.
Why sure their Generation was asleepe,
When shee begot those Dormice; that shee made
Them vp so weakely and imperfectly.
One wants desire; the tother habilitie.
When my affection euen with their cold blouds
(As snow rub'd through an actiue hand, does make
The flesh to burne) by agitation is
Inflam'd. I could vnbrace, and entertaine
The ayre to coole it.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: That but mitigates
The heate; rather imbrace and entertaine
A younger brother; he can quench the fire.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Can you so, sir? now I beshrew your eare.
Why bold Sebastian, how dare you approach
So neare the presence of your displeas'd Father.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Vnder the protection of his present absence.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Belike you knew he was abroad then.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Yes.
Let me encounter you so; Ile perswade
Your meanes to reconcile me to his loue.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Is that the way? I vnderstand you not.
But for your reconcilement, meete m'at home;
Ile satisfie your suite

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Within this halfe houre?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Lust is a Spirit, which whosoe'er doth raise;
The next man that encounters boldly, layes.
prose:
Or within this whole houre. When you will.—
A lusty bloud! has both the presence and the spirit of a man.
I like the freedome of his behauiour.—Ho—Sebastian!
Gone?—Has set my bloud o'boyling i'my veynes And now
(like water pour'd vpon the ground, that mixes it selfe with
eu'ry moysture it meetes) I could claspe with any man.

O Fresco! Art thou come? If tother faile, then thou art entertaind.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Such stones men vse to raise a house vpon;
But with these stones I goe to ruine one.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Passion o'me you drunken knaues: you'l put the lights out.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: No my Lord; th'are but in ieast.
Mine's out.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Then light it at his head, that's light enough.—
Foregod, th'are out. You drunken Rascals backe and light'em.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: T'is exceeding darke.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
No matter. I am acquainted with the way. Your hand.
Let's easily walke. Ile lead you till they come.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose:
My soule's opprest with griefe^ T'lies heauie at my
heart, O my departed Sonne! ere long I shall be with ^

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Marry God forbid.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: O, o, o.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Now all the hoste of heauen forbid. Knaues, Rogues.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Pray God hee be not hurt! her's falne into the grauell pit.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Brother! deare Brother! Rascals, villaines, knaues.

Eternall darkenesse damne you; come away. Goe round about
into the grauell pit, and helpe my Brother vp. Why what a
strange vnlucky night ^ this? Is't not my Lord? I thinke that
Dogge that ho^l'd the newes of griefe, that fatall Scrichowle
vsherd on this mischiefs.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Mischeife indeed my Lord. Your Brother's dead.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Hee's dead.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Hee's dead.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Dead be your tongues. Drop out mine eye-bals, and
let enuious Fortune play at tennis with'em. Haue I liu'd to this?
Malicious Nature! hadst thou borne me blinde; th'adst yet been
something fauourable to me. No breath? No motion? 'prithee
tell me heauen! hast shut thine eye to winke at murther; or hast
put this sable garment on, to mourne at's death? Not one poore
sparke in the whole spatious skye, of all that endlesse number
would vouchsafe to shine? You vize-royes to the King of nature!
whose constellations gouerne mortall births; where is
that fatall Planet rul'd at his Natiu^tie? That might ha'pleas'd
to light him out, as well into th'world; vnlesse it be asham'd

T^haue beene the instrument of such a good mans cursed dest^nie.—

verse: Passions transports you. Recollect your selfe.
^ him not. Whether our deaths be good
Or bad; it is not death but life that tryes;
Hee liu'd well, (therefore) questionlesse, well dyes.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
I. Tis an easie thing for him that has no paine to talke
of patience. Doe you thinke that Nature has no feeling?

speeches.speaker: Belf.
prose:
Feeling? Yes. But has she purpos'd any thing for nothing?
What good receiues this body by your griefe? Whether
is't more vnnaturall not to grieue for him you cannot
helpe with it; or hurt your selfe with grieuing and yet grieue
in vaine?

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Indeede had hee beene taken from mee like a piece
o'dead flesh, I should neither ha' felt it, nor grieued for't. But
come hether, 'pray looke heere. Behold the liuely tincture of
his bloud! Neither the Dropsie nor the Iaundies in't. But the
true freshnesse of a sanguine red; for all the fogge of this blacke
murdrous night has mix'd with it. For any thing I know, hee
might ha' liu'd till doomesday, and ha' done more good then either
you or I. O Brother ^ He was a man of such a natiue goodnesse;
as if Regeneration had beene giuen him in his mothers
wombe. So harmeles, that rather then ha' trod vpon a worme,
hee would ha' shun'd the way. So deerely pittifull, that e're the
poore could aske his charity with dry eyes, hee gaue' em reliefe
wi'teares—with teares—yes faith with teares.

speeches.speaker: Belf.
prose:
Take vp the Corps. For wisedom's sake let reason fortifie
this weakenesse.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Why what would you ha' mee doe? Foolish Nature
will haue her course in spight o'wisedome. But I haue e'en
done. All these wordes were but a great winde, and now this
showre of teares has layd it, I am calme againe. You may set forward
when you will. Ile follow you, like one that must and
would not.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose: Our opposition will but trouble him.

speeches.speaker: Belf.
prose:
The griefe that melts to teares, by it selfe is spent,
Passion resisted, growes more violent.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Here's a sweete Comedie. T'begins with O dolentis,
and concludes with ha, ha, he.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Ha, ha, he.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
O my eccho! I could stand reuerberating this sweete
musicall ayre of ioy, till I had perish'd my sound lungs with
violent laughter. Louely Night-Rauen! th'ast seaz'd a carkasse.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose:
Put him out on's paine. I lay so fitly vnderneath the
bancke from whence he fell; that e'er his faltring tongue could
vtter double Oo; I knock'd out's braines with this fai^e
Rubie. And had another stone iust of this forme and bignesse
ready: that I laid i'the broken skull vpo'the ground for's pillow;
against the which they thought he fell and perish'd.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Vpon this ground Ile build my Manour-house;
And this shall be the chiefest corner stone.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: T'has crown'd the most iudicious murder, that
The braine of man was e'er deliuer'd of.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: I. Marke the plot. Not any circumstance
That stood within the reach of the designe,
Of persons, dispositions, matter, time or place,
But by this braine of mine, was made
An Instrumentall help; yet nothing from
Th'induction to th'accomplishment seem'd forc'd,
Or done o'purpose, but by accident.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: First, my report that Charlemont was dead,
Though false; yet couer'd with a masque of truth.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: I, and deliuer'd in as fit a time.
When all our mindes so wholy were possess'd
With one affaire, that no man would suspect
A thought imploi'd for any second end.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Then the Precisian to be ready, when
Your brother spake of death, to moue his Will.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: His businesse cal'd him thither; and it fell
Within his office; vnrequested to't.
From him it came religiously; and sau'd
Our proiect from suspition: which if I
Had mou'd had beene endanger'd.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Then your healths.
Though seeming but the ordinarie rites,
And ceremonies due to fest^uals:—

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Yet vs'd by me to make the seruants drunke.
An instrument the plot could not haue miss'd.
T'was easie to set drunkards by the eares:
Th'ad nothing but their torches to fight with;
And when those lights were out;

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Then darkenesse did
Protect the execution of the worke,
Both from preuention and discouerie.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Here was a murther brauely carryed, through
The eye of obseruation, vnobseru'd.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: And those that saw the passage of it, made
The Instruments yet knew not what they did.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: That power of rule Philosophers ascribe
To him they call the supreame of the Starres;
Making their influences gouernours
Of Sublunarie Creatures; when their selues
Are senselesse of their operations.
prose:
What! Doest start at thunder? Credit my beliefe, t'is a meere
effect of nature. An exhalation hot and dry, inuolu'd within a
watrie vapour i'the middle religion of the ayre. Whose coldnesse
congealing that thicke moysture to a cloud: the angry
exhalation shut within a prison of contrary qualitie, striues to
be free; and with the violent eruption through the grossenesse
of that cloud; makes this noyse we heare.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: T'is a fearefull noyse.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
T'is a braue noyse. And mee thinkes graces our accomplishid
proiect, as a peale of Ordnance does a triumph. It
speakes encouragement. Now Nature showes thee how it sauour'd
our performance; to forbeare this noyse when wee set
forth, because it should not terrifie my brothers going home;
which would haue dash'd our purpose: To forbeare this lightning
in our passage, least it should ha'warn'd him o'the
pitfall. Then propitious Nature winck'd at our proceedings;

now it doth expresse, how that forbearance fauour'd our successe.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You haue confirm'd mee. For it followes well;
That Nature (since her selfe decay doth hate)
Should fauour those that strengthen their estate.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Our next endeauour is; since on the false report that
Charlemont is dead, depends the fabrique of the worke; to credit
that with all the countenance wee can.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose:
Faith Sir, euen let his owne inheritance, whereof y'aue
dispossess'd him, countenance the act. Spare so much out of
that, to giue him a solempnitie of funerall. T'will quit the cost;
and make your apprehension of his death appeare more confident
and true.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Ile take thy counsell. Now farewell blacke night;
Thou beauteous Mistresse of a murderer:
To honour thee, that hast accomplish'd all;
Ile weare thy colours at his funerall.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Th'art welcome into my chamber; Fresco. Prithee
shut the dore.—Nay thou mistakest me. Come in and
shut it.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: T'is somewhat late Madame.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
No matter. I haue somewhat to say to thee. What? is
not thy mistresse towards a husband yet?

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
Faith Madame, shee has suitors. But they will not suite
her me thinkes. They will not come off lustily it seemes.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: They will not come on lustily, thou wouldst say.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: I meane (Madame) they are not rich enough.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
But I (Fresco) they are not bold enough. Thy Mistresse
is of a liuely attractiue bloud Fr^ sco. And in troth shee's
o'my minde for that. A poore spirit is poorer then a poore
purse.
Give me a fellow that brings not onely temptation with
him, but has the actiuitie of wit, and audacitie of spirit to apply
euery word and gesture of a womans speech and behauiour to
his owne desire; and make her beleeue shee's the suitor her selfe.
Neuer giue backe till he has made her yeeld to 'it.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
Indeede among our equals Madame; but otherwise we
shall be put horribly out o'countenance.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Thou art deceiu'd, Fresco. Ladyes are as cou^teous as
Yeomens wiue^, and me thinkes they should be more gentle.
Hot diet and soft ease makes em (like waxe alwaies kept warme)
more easie to take impression.—Prithee vntie my shooe.
—What? art thou shamefac'd too? Goe roundly to worke
man. My legge is not goutie: t'will endure the feeling I warrant
thee Come hither Fresco; thine eare.—S'daintie; I mistooke
the place. I miss'd thine eare and hit thy lip.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: Your Lad^ship has made me blush.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
That showes th'art full o'lustie bloud^ and thou knowest
not how to vse it. Let mee see thy hand. Thou shouldst not
be shamefac'd by thy hand, Fresco. Here's a brawny flesh and a
hairy skinne: both signes of an able body. I doe not like these
flegmaticke, smooth-skinn'd, soft-flesh'd fellowes. They are
like candied Suckets, when they begin to perish; which I would
alwayes emptie my Closet off, and giue'em my chamber-maid.
—I haue some skill in Palmestry: by this line that stands directly
against mee; thou shouldst be neare a good fortune.
Fresco, if thou hadst the grace to entertaine it.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: O what is that Madame? I pray!

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
No lesse then the loue of a faire Lady, if thou doest not
lose her with faint-heartednesse.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
A Lady, Madame? alas a Lady is a great thing, I cannot
compasse her.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: No? Why? I am a Lady, Am I so great I cannot be compassed? Claspe my wast and try.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: I could finde i'my heart Madame.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Vds body; my Husband! Faint-hearted foole! I thinke
thou wert begotten betweene the North-pole, and the congeal'd
passage. Now like an ambitious Coward that betrayes
himselfe with fearefull delay: you must suffer for the treason
you neuer committed. Goe hide thy selfe behind yound'arras,
instantly.

Sebastian! What doe you here so late?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: Nothing yet; but I hope I shall.—

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Y'are very bold.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: And you very valiant; for you met mee at full Cariere.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
You come to ha'me moue your fathers reconciliation.
Ile write a word or two i'your behalfe.

speeches.speaker: Seba
prose:
A word or two, Madame? that you doe for mee, will
not be contain'd in lesse then the compasse of two sheetes. But
in plaine termes, shall wee take the opportunitie of priuatenesse?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: What to doe?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
To dance the beginning of the world after the English
manner.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Why not after the French or Italian?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: Fie. They dance it preposterously; backward.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Are you so actiue to dance?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: I can shake my heeles.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Y'are well made for't.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Measure me from top to toe; you shall not finde mee
differ much from the true standard of proportion.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
I thinke I am accurs'd. Sebastian! There's one at the
doore has beaten opportunitie away from vs. In briefe, I loue
thee. And it shall not be long before I giue thee a testimony of
it. To saue thee now from suspition; doe no more but draw thy
Rapier; chase thy selfe; and when hee comes in, rush by without
taking notice of him. Onely seeme to be angry, and let me
alone for the rest.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: Now by the hand of M^rcurie.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: What's the matter wife?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Ooh, Ooh, Husband!

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Prithee what ail'st thou woman?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
O feele my pulse. It beates I warrant you. Be patient
a little sweet Husband; tarry but till my breath come to me againe,
and Ile satisfie you.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: What a^les Sebastian, he lookes so distractedly?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
The poore Gentleman's almost out on's wits I thinke.
You remember the displeasure his Father tooke against him
about the liberty of speech he vs'd euen now when your daughter
went to be marryed.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Yes, what of that?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
T'has craz'd him sure: he met a poore man i'the street
euen now. Vpou what quarrell I know not: but hee pursued
him so violently, that if my house had not beene his rescue; he
had surely ki^d him.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: What a strange desperate young man is that!

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Nay husband, hee grew so in rage when hee saw the
man was conueyed from him, that he was ready euen to haue
drawne his naked weapon vpon mee. And had not your knocking
at the doore preuented him; surely h'ad done something
to mee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Where's the man?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose:
Alas here. I warrant you the poore fearefull soule is
scarce come to himselfe againe yet.—If the foole haue
any wit hee will apprehend mee.—Doe you heare sir^
You may be bold to come forth; the Fury that haunted you
is gone.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: Are you sure hee is gone?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Hee's gone; hee's gone, I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
I would I were gone too. Has shooke mee almost into
a dead palsie.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: How fell the difference betweene you?

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: I would I were out at the backe doore.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Th'art safe enough. Prithee tell's the falling out.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
Yes sir, when I haue recouered my spirits. My memory
is almost frighted from mee.—Oh so, so, so.—
Why Sir, as I came along the streete Sir;—this same Gentleman
came stumbling after mee, and trod o'my hecle,—

I cryed O. Doe you cry sirrah? saies hee. Let mee see your
heele; if it be not hurt, Ile make you cry for something. So he
claps my head betweene his legges, and pulles off my shooe.
I hauing shifted no sockes in a sea' night, the Gentleman cryed
foh; and said my feete were base and cowardly feete, they
stuncke for feare. Then hee knock'd my shooe about my pate,
and I cryed O, once more. In the meane time comes a shag.
hair'd dogge by, and rubbes against his shinnes. The Gentleman
tooke the dog in shagge-haire to be some Watch-man in
a rugge gowne; and swore hee would hang mee vp at the next
doore with my lanthorne in my hand, th^t passengers might
see their way as they went without rubbing against Gentlemens
shinnes. So, for want of a Cord. hee tooke his owne
garters off; and as he was going to make a nooze, I watch'd my
time and ranne away. And as I ranne (indeede) I bid him hang
himselfe in his owne gatters. So hee in choler, puisued mee hither
as you see.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Why this sauours of distraction.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Of meere distraction.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose: How soeuer it sauours, I am sure it smels like a lye.

speeches.speaker: Bel
prose:
Thou maist goe forth at the backe doore (honest fellow)
the way is priuate and safe.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
So it had neede, for your fore-doore (here) is both
common and dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Good night honest Fresco.

speeches.speaker: Fres.
prose:
Good night Madame; if you get mee kissing o'Ladies
againe.—

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: This fals out handsomely.
But yet the matter does not well succeed;
Till I haue brought it to the very deede.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Serieant! what houre o'the night is't.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: About one.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: I would you would relieue me; for I am
So heauie, that I shall ha'much adoe;
To stand out my perdu.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Ile e'en but walke
The round (sir) and then presently returne.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
prose:
For God's sake Serieant relieue me, aboue fiue houres
together in so foule a stormy night as this?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose:
Why t'isa musique Souldier. Heauen and earth are now
in consort, when the Thunder and the Canon play one to another.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose:
I know not why I should be thus inclin'd to sleepe, I
feele my disposition press'd with a necessitie of heauines. Souldier!
if thou hast any better eyes, I prithee wake mee when the Serieant comes.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
prose:
Sir, t'is so darke and stormy that I shall scarce eyther see
or heare him e'er he comes vpon mee.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: I cannot ^orce my selfe to wake.—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Returne to France; for thy old Father's dead;
And thou by murther, disinherited.
Attend with patience the successe of things;
But leaue reuenge vnto the King of kings.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: O my affrighted soule! what fearefull dreame
Was this that wak'd mee? Dreames are but the rais'd
Impressions of premeditated things,
By serious apprehension left vpon
Our mindes, or else th'imaginary shapes
Of obiects proper to th' complexion, or
The dispositions of our bodyes. These
Can neyther of them be the cause, why I
Should dreame thus; for my mind has not been mou'd
With any one conception of a thought
To such a purpose; nor my nature wont
To trouble me with phantasies of terror.
It must be something that my Genius would
Informe me of. Now gratious heauen forbid!
O! let my Spirit be depriu'd of all
Fore-sight and knowledge, ere it vnderstand
That vision acted; or diuine that act
To come. Why should I thinke so? Left I not
My worthy Father i'the kind regard
Of a most louing Vncle? Souldier! sawst
No apparition of a man?

speeches.speaker: Soul.
prose: You dreame Sir; I saw nothing.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Tush. These idle dreames
Are fabulous. Our boyling phantasies
Like troubled waters falsifie the shapes
Of things retain'd in them; and make' em seeme
Confounded, when they are distinguish'd, So
My actions daily conuersant with warre;
(The argument of bloud and death) had left
(Perhaps) th'imaginary presence of
Some bloudy accident vpon my minde:
Which mix'd confusedly with other thoughts,
(Whereof th'remembrance of my Father, might
Be one) presented all together, seeme
Incorporate; as if his body were
The owner of that bloud, the subiect of
That death; when hee's at Paris, and that bloud
Shed here. It may be thus. I would not leaue
The warre, for reputatio'ns sake, vpon
An idle apprehension; a vaine dreame.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
prose:
Stand. Stand, I say. No? Why then haue at thee. Sir,
if you will not stand, Ile make you fall? Nor stand, nor fall?
Nay then the Diuel's damme has broke her husbands head: for
sure it is a Spirit, I shot it through, and yet it will not fall.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: O pardon me! my doubtfull heart was slow
To credit that which I did feare to know.

speeches.speaker: D'amville.
verse: SEt downe the Body. Pay earth what shee lent.
But shee shall beare a liuing monument,
To let succeeding ages truely know.
That shee is satisfied, what hee did owe:
Both principall and vse; because his worth
Was better at his death then at his birth.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: And with his Body, place that memorie
Of noble Charlemont his worthie Sonne.
And giue their Graues the rites that doe belong
To Souldiers. They were Souldiers both. The Father
Held open warre with Sinne; the Sonne with bloud:
This in a warre more gallant^ that more good.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: There place their Armes; and here their Epitaphe^.
And may these Lines suruiue the last of graues.
HEre lye the Ashes of that earth and fire;
whose heat and fruit, ded feede and warme the poore ^
And they (as if they would in sighes expire,
and into teares dissolue) his death deplore.
Hee did that good freel^ for goodnesse sake,
fnforc'd: for gen'rousnesse he held so deare,
That hee fear'd none but him that did him make,
and yet he seru'd him more for loue then feare.
So's life prouided, that though he did dye
Asod^une death; yet dyed not sodainely.
HIs Body lies interr'd within this would;
Who dyed a young man, yet departed old.
And in all strength of youth that Man can haue,
Was ready still to drop into his graue.
For ag'd in vertue with a youthfull eye,
He welcom'd it being still prepar'd to dye;
And liuing so, though young depriu'd of breath,
He did not suffer an vntimely death.
But we may say of his braue bless'd decease ^
He dyed in warre; and yet hee dyed in peace.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: O might that fire reuiue the ashes of
This Phenix! yet the wonder would not be
So great as he was good; and wondred at
For that. His liues example was so true
A practique of Religion's Theorie;
That her Diuinitie seem'd rather the
Description then th'instruction of his life.
And of his goodnesse, was his vertuous Sonne
A worthy imitatour. So that on
These two Herculean pillars, where their armes
Are plac'd; there may be writ, Non vltra. For
Beyond their liues as well for youth as age;
Nor young nor old, in merit or in name;
Shall e'er exceede their vertues or their fame.
T'is done. Thus faire accomplements, make foule
Deedes gratious. Charlemont! come now when t'wut.
I'ue buryed vnder these two marble stones.
Thy liuing hopes; And thy dead fathers bones.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O thou that knowest me iustly Charl^monts.
Though in the forc'd possession of another;
Since from thine owne free spirit wee receiue it,
That our aff^ctions cannot be compel'd,
Though' our actions may; be not displeas'd, if on
The altar of his Tombe, I sacrifice
My teares. They are the iewels of my loue
Dissolued ^ to griefe: and fall vpon
His blasted Spring; as Aprill dewe, vpon
A sweet young blossome shak'd before the time.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Goe see my Truncks disposed of, Ile but walk
A turne or two i'th Church and follow you.
O! here's the fatall monument of my
Dead Father first presented to mine eye.
What's here? in memory of Charlemont?
Some false relation has abus'd beliefe.
I am deluded. But I thanke thee Heauen.
For euer let me be deluded thus.
My Castabella mourning o'er my Hearse?
Sweete Castab^lla rise, I am not dead.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O heauen defend mee.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: I Beshrew my rash
And inconsid'rate passion.—Castabella!
That could not thinke—my Castabella!—that
My sodaine presence might affright her sense.—
I prithee (my affection) pardon mee.
Reduce thy vnderstanding to thine eye.
Within this habite which thy misinform'd
Conceipt takes onely for a shape; liue both
The soule and body of thy Charlemont.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: I feele a substance, warme, and soft, and moist,
Subiect to the capacitie of sense.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Which Spirits are not; for their effence is
Aboue the nature and the order of
Those Elements whereof our senses are
Created. Touch my lip. Why turnst thou from mee?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Griefe aboue g^iefes. That which should woe relieue,
Wish'd and obtain'd, giues greater cause to grieue.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Can Castabella thinke it cause of griefe
That the relation of my death proues false?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: The presence of the person wee affect,
(Being hopelesse to enioy him) makes our griefe
More passionate then if wee saw him not.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Why not enioy? has absence chang'd thee?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Yes.
From maide to wife.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Art marryed?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: O I am.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Married had not my mother been a woman,
I should protest against the chastitie
Of all thy sexe. How can the Marchant, or
The Marriner absent whole yeares (from wiues
Exper^enc'd in the satisfaction of
Desire) promise themselues to finde their sheetes
Vnspotted with adultery, at their
Returne? when you that neuer had the sense
Of actuall temptation; could not stay
A few short months.

speeches.speaker: Caste.
verse: O doe but heare me speake.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: But thou wert wise; and didst consider that
A Souldier might be maim'd, and so (perhaps)
Lose his habilitie to please thee.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: No. That weaknes pleases me in him I have.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: What? marryed to a man vnable too?
O strange incontinence! Why? was thy bloud
Increas'd to such a pleurisie of lust,
That of necessitie, there must a veyne
Be open'd; though by one that had no skill
To doe't?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Sir, I beseech you heare me.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Speake.

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Heau'n knowes I am vnguiltie of this act.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Why? wer't thou forc'd to doe't?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Heau'n knowes I was.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: What villaine did it?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Your Vncle 'D'amville.
And he that dispossess'd my loue of you;
Hath disinherited you of possession.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Disinherited? wherein haue I deseru'd
To be depriu'd of my deare Fathers loue?

speeches.speaker: Casta.
verse: Both of his loue and him. His soule's at rest.
But here your iniur'd patience may behold
The signes of his lamented memorie.
H'as found it. When I tooke him for a Ghoast,
I could endure the torment of my feare;
More eas'ly then I can his sorrowes heare.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Of all mens griefes must mine be singular?
Without example? Heere I met my graue.
And all mens woes are buried i' their graues
But mine. In mine my miseries are borne.
I pr'ithee sorrow leaue a little roome,
In my confounded and tormented mind;
For vnderstanding to deliberate
The cause or author of this accident.—
A close aduantage of my absence made,
To dispossesse me both of land and wife:
And all the profit does arise to him,
By whom my absence was first mou'd and vrg'd.
These circumstances (Vncle) tell me, you
Are the suspected author of those wrongs.
Whereof the lightest, is more heauie then
The strongest patience can endure to beare.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Now Sir! your businesse?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: My Annuitie.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Not a deniere.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: How would you ha'me liue?

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Why turne Cryer. Cannot you turne Cryer?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Then doe so, y'haue a good voice for't.
Y'are excellent at crying of a Rape.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Sir, I confesse in particular respect to your selfe, I
was somewhat forgetfull. Gen'rall honestie possess'd me.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Goe, th'art the base corruption of my bloud;
And like a Tetter growes't vnto my flesh.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Inflict any punishment vpon me. The seueritie shall
not discourage me, if it be not shamefull; so you'l but put money
i'my purse. The want of money makes a free spirit more
mad then the possession does an Vsurer.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Not a farthing.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Would you ha'me turne purse-taker? T'is the next
way to doe't. For want is like the Racque; it drawes a man to
endanger himselfe to the gallowes rather then endure it.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
What art thou? Stay. Assist my troubled sence.
My apprehension will distract me. Stay.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: What art thou? speake.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: The spirit of Charlemont.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: O stay! compose me. I dissolue.

speeches.speaker: Lang.
prose:
No. T'is prophane. Spirits are inuisible. T'is the fiend
i'the likenesse of Charlemont. I will haue no conuersation with
Sathan.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: The Spirit of Charlemont? I'le try that.
'Fore God thou sayest true, th'art all Spirit.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
verse: Goe call the Officers.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Th'art a villaine; and the Sonne of a villaine.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: You lye.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Haue at thee.
Reuenge to thee Ile dedicate this worke.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Hold Charlemont!
Let him reuenge my murder, and thy wrongs,
To whom the lustice of Reuenge belongs.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
You torture me betweene the passion of my bloud,
and the religion of my soule,

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose: A good honest fellow.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
What? wounded? apprehend him. Sir; is this your
salutation for the courtesie I did you when wee parted last?
You ha'forgot I lent you a thousand Crownes. First, let him
aunswere for this riot. When the Law is satisfied for that; an
an action for his debt shall clap him vp againe. I tooke you
for a Spirit; and Ile coniure you before I ha'done.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose:
No. Ile turne Coniurer. Diuell! within this Circle,
in the midst of all thy force and malice I coniure thee doe thy
worst.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose: Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Sir, I haue got a scratch or two here for your sake. I
hope you'l giue mee money to pay the Surgeon.

speeches.speaker: D'am.
prose:
Borachio! fetch me a thousand Crownes. I am content
to countenance the freedome of your spirit when t'is worthily
imployed. A Gods name giue behauiour the full scope of
gen'rous libertie; but let it not disperse and spend it selfe in
courses of vnbounded licence. Here, pay for your hurts.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
I thanke you sir.—Gen'rous libertie.—that
is to say, freely to bestow my habilities to honest purposes. Me
thinkes I should not follow that instruction now; if hauing the

meanes to doe an honest office for an honest fellow, I should
neglect it. Charlemont lyes in prison for a thousand Crownes.
And here I haue a thousand Crownes. Honestie tels meet'were
well done to release Charlemont. But discretion sayes I had
much a doe to come by this; and when this shall be gone I
know not where to singer any more: especially if I employ it
to this vse, which is like to endanger mee into my Fathers perpetuall
displeasure. And then I may goe hang my selfe, or be
forc'd to doe that, will make another saue mee the labour. No
matter. Charlemont! Thou gau'st mee my life and that's somewhat
of a purer earth then gold as fine as it is. T'is no courtesie
I doe thee but thankefulnesse. I owe thee it and Ile pay it.
Hee sought brauely, but the Officers drag'd him villanously.
Arrant knaues! for vsing him so discourtcously; may the sins
o'the poore people be so few, that you sha'not be able to spare
so much out o'your gettings, as will pay for the hyre of a lame
staru'd hackney to ride to an execution. But goe a foote to the
gallowes, and be hang'd. May elder brothers turne good husbands,
and younger brothers get good wiues; that there be no
neede of debt-bookes, nor vse of Serieants. May there be all
peace but i'the warre, and all charitie but i'the Diuell; so that
prisons may be turn'd to Hospitals, though the Officers liue
othe beneuolence. If this curse might come to passe, the world
would say, Blessed be he that curseth.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: I graunt the Heauen. Thy goodnesse doth command
Our punishments: but yet no further then
The measure of our sinnes. How should they else
Be iust? Or how should that good purpose of
Thy Iustice take effect, by bounding men
Within the confines of humanitie,
When our afflictions doe exceede our crimes?
Then they doe rather teach the barb'rous world
Examples that extend her cruelties
Beyond their owne dimentions; and instruct
Our actions to be more, more barbarous.
O my afflicted soule! How torment swels
Thy apprehension with prophane conceipt,
Against the sacred iustice of my God?
Our owne constructions are the authors of
Our miserie. We neuer measure our
Conditions but with Men aboue vs in
Estate. So while our Spirits labour to
Be higher then our fortunes th'are more base.
Since all those attributes which make men seeme
Superiour to vs; are Man's Subiects; and
Were made to serue him. The repining Man
Is of a seruile spirit to deiect
The valew of himselfe below their estimation.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
prose:
Here. Take my sword.—How now my wilde
Swag'rer? y'are tame enough now; are you not? The penurie
of a prison is like a soft consumption. T'will humble the pride
o' your mortalitie; and arme your soule in compleate patience
to endure the waight of affliction without feeling it. What?
Hast no musicke in thee? Th'hast trebles and bases enough.
Treble iniurie; and base vsage. But trebles and bases make
poore musick without meanes. Thou want'st Meanes; Doest?
what? Doest droope? art deiected?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: No Sir. I haue a heart aboue the reach
Of thy most violent maliciousnesse.
A fortitude in scorne of thy contempt;
(Since Fate is pleas'd to haue me suffer it)
That can beare more then thou hast power t'inflict.
I was a Baron That thy Father has
Depriu'd me off. In stead of that, I am
Created King. I'ue lost a Signiorie,
That was confin'd within a piece of earth;
A Wart vpon the body of the world.
